carolyn-m1: Yeast and the lake. That’s the honest answer. Mom baked bread every Saturday whether we needed it or not, and our house sat four blocks from Lake Macatawa, close enough that when the wind came off the water it went right through the screen door. I was the middle of three, wedged between Tom, who was always in trouble, and Anne, who never was, because Tom used it all up.
carolyn-m2: Tell Ellie it was Tulip Time, 1968. I was eight. First year dancing. You know the wooden shoes? Klompen. They’re heavy and they do not bend. Mom sewed my costume at the kitchen table for three weeks: the white cap, the striped apron, all of it. I practiced in the driveway in my wooden shoes until the neighbors begged. Halfway down Eighth Street my left klomp just flew.
carolyn-m8: The moon. Grandpa’s front room. I was nine. Grandpa Walsh had the only set on our street that got Channel 8 without tinfoil on the antenna, so everybody came. Oh, it was packed. The kids sat on the rug and the grown-ups stood along the wall with their arms crossed, like they were in church. When the man stepped down, nobody said a word.
carolyn-m3: It rained. Oh, it rained. From six in the morning until nine at night. Every aunt I had said rain on your wedding day is good luck, and I wanted to throw something at all of them. The tent leaked right over the head table. And Rick, without saying a word, just picked up an umbrella and held it over me for the whole dinner. Ate with his left hand.
carolyn-m5: The beach one. Tunnel Park, 1986. Anne took it. I’m holding Dylan and I look like I haven’t slept in a year, which I hadn’t. We spent every summer weekend out there. Egg salad sandwiches, those terrible orange sodas Dylan loved, and we’d stay until the lifeguard went home. She was two and sure she could walk into Lake Michigan and keep going.
carolyn-m4: Dylan arrived on a Tuesday in March of 1984, three weeks early and furious about it. Rick drove us home from Holland Hospital at about eleven miles an hour. People were honking. He didn’t care. I kissed that cheek ten thousand times, and every one felt like the first. The summer she turned three, Rick built her an easel from scrap he brought home from the plant.
carolyn-m11: Yes, honey. March 1989. Your mom had pneumonia and they kept her at Holland Hospital for six nights. I slept in the chair. Grandpa brought me clothes and a thermos of coffee every morning. I learned that being scared and being brave happen at the same time. You don’t get to wait for one to finish. And Ellie, she was fine. She’s your mother. She still hates hospitals.
carolyn-m10: 1996. The oven died at eleven in the morning with a twenty-two-pound turkey in it. Dylan says twenty. Rick says eighteen. It was twenty-two. I bought it. Panic, for about a minute. Then I thought, well, I own two big ovens. So we cut it into pieces and cooked it in the bakery ovens.
carolyn-m6: Honestly? I was tired of making someone else’s bread. I’d worked the counter at other places since I was seventeen. And Mom’s recipes were better. That’s not pride, that’s just true. I was thirty-four and scared to death. We put the house up to borrow the money. Rick didn’t blink. He painted the sign himself, on our garage floor. It said Ruth’s Table and the R was a little crooked.
carolyn-m7: That winter I took Mom a loaf every morning before we opened. Rye, if it was warm; she could manage rye. One morning in January she didn’t eat any. She held it in her lap like a cat. I cried in the van after and I didn’t tell Rick. By February she slept most of the day. I baked her lemon cake anyway, so the house would smell right.
carolyn-m9: I’d like to say church. It wasn’t. I stopped going for a while. I was angry, and I didn’t want to sit there being angry in a nice dress. What carried me was the Saturdays. The cards. My hands knew what to do even when I didn’t. I suppose that was a kind of praying. Pastor Jim said so, anyway, when I went back. Easter, 2018.
carolyn-m12: Coffee, the crossword, one call from Dylan, and bread in the oven. That’s a good day. I don’t need much more than that anymore. I think about the Saturdays at Tunnel Park, the four-loaf days, Mom leaning on the counter. You don’t get told which ones are the ones. Ellie’s coming at ten. I should go find the next card.
raymond-m1: My father fixed cars on South Flores Street. Six kids, one bay, and a sign he painted himself. Ortiz Auto. No first name on it, because he said the name was the family’s, not his. I was the fourth boy. The three older ones got the wrenches. I got the broom, and then the parts washer, and then, when I was eleven, the caliper. Six-inch dial, Brown and Sharpe.
raymond-m2: I was supposed to finish high school. I finished most of it. In the spring of 1968 a man named Walt Brenner came into my father’s bay with a Pontiac that wouldn’t idle, and while my father fixed it he watched me deburr a bracket with a file. He had a job shop on Roosevelt Avenue, eleven men, and he needed a kid to sweep. A dollar sixty an hour.
raymond-m3: My first Michigan paycheck was for sixty-one hours. I didn’t have a bank. The foreman said go to the credit union on Division, they’ll take anybody. There were three windows and two were open. I picked the one with the girl who wasn’t smiling. That was Elena. She looked at my deposit slip, looked at me, and said, you added this wrong. I had. By four dollars, in my favor.
raymond-m13: Elena made one rule when we started the shop. The first week of August, the doors close, everybody paid, nobody in the building. Especially me. Once we could afford it, every August we rented the same cottage on Spring Lake. I couldn’t swim. Where I grew up the pool on our side of town was closed more than it was open, and then I was working.
raymond-m6: I had a good job. I was the best setup man at a tool and die shop on the southwest side, and I knew it, and so did they. What I couldn’t stand was watching parts go out late because nobody upstairs would listen to the floor.
raymond-m4: Your grandmother was the most important person in that company, and nobody knew it. That’s not even a question. For twenty-one years, most nights after the kids were down and all day Sunday, she sat at this table with a green ledger, a pencil and an adding machine. Everything with a dollar sign. She chased the late invoices. She handled the bank.
raymond-m7: By spring of ’84 I had more work than hands. I put a card on the board at the hardware store on Division. Machinist wanted, must own tools. Three men called. Two wanted to know the pay first. Hector Ruiz asked what I was making. Brackets, I said. He asked what tolerance. I told him, and he said, on a Bridgeport?
raymond-m14: My father came north once. June 1985, on the Greyhound, because he didn’t trust airplanes or my driving. I wanted him to see the garage on Godfrey Avenue, the mill, the work on the board, the sign. He walked around it a long time and didn’t say anything. Then he found Elena’s mother’s fan on my bench and fixed it.
raymond-m8: The most expensive mistake I ever made came in on a Tuesday in 1986, and it looked like the best day of my life. Twelve thousand brackets a month for a big office-furniture maker on the lakeshore. One purchase order. I hired four people that week and bought a second mill on credit. By 1988 we were twelve people in a real building.
raymond-m9: It was February 8, 1991, a Friday, two weeks after the call from the lakeshore. Fourteen people, and the money for payroll wasn’t there. I’d done the arithmetic four times and it came out the same four times. I sat in the truck in the parking lot for an hour. I didn’t go in.
raymond-m5: Nobody in this family talks about 2019, so I’ll go first. Tomás wanted to run the company. He’d been on the floor since he was sixteen and in the office since 2008, and he was ready. I said not yet. I said it in 2014 and I said it in 2016 and I’m told I said it a few more times after that.
raymond-m11: The private equity offer was the better deal on paper. I’m not going to pretend otherwise. In the end I took about a fifth less and sold the company to the people who worked there. An employee stock ownership plan. A piece of it for every one of them.
raymond-m12: I go in on Thursdays. Nobody asked me to and nobody’s told me to stop. I walk the floor before anybody’s read their email, the way I always did, and I say good morning to a hundred and forty people and I don’t know all their names anymore. Then I stand by the Bridgeport for a while. It’s at the front of the shop.
tom-m1: We lived two blocks from the foundry where my dad worked, on a street where every house put a flag out on the Fourth of July. I was nineteen, pumping gas and taking one class at the community college, which was not enough to keep me out. The letter came on a Tuesday in April.
tom-m2: I bought the Chevy at seventeen with gas-station money. A ’57, two-tone, turquoise and white, and it burned oil the whole time I had it. Friday nights everybody drove Genesee Avenue, up to the river and back, up to the river and back. You weren’t going anywhere. That was the point. My father didn’t say much about it. He checked the tires. That was how he said things.
tom-m3: I met Diane at the St. Joseph’s picnic, the July before I left. She was pouring lemonade and I went back three times. The third time she said, you don’t even like lemonade, and I said no. That was the whole courtship. One afternoon. I had the letter already. I told her the date. She said, write me the address when you have one. I didn’t think she meant it.
tom-m4: They trained me for ten weeks to be a medic, and in February 1968 they put me on a plane. I landed ten days after Tết started. By the end of my first week everybody in the company called me Doc. Nobody used my name for a year. The first man I treated was older than me by a month. I remember his boots, not his face.
tom-m5: Danny Alvarez. From Corpus Christi. We went through training together and ended up in the same company by dumb luck. He laughed louder than anyone I ever met. He had a girl at home too, and we’d read each other’s letters out loud, the parts you could read. May 1968. It was a Monday, the sixth. I know because I’d crossed off the fifth that morning. I got to him.
tom-m6: Mail came when it came. Sometimes nothing for two weeks and then a bundle with a rubber band around it, and you’d sort them by the postmark so you read them in order. Diane wrote every week. Every single week, for a year, to a boy she’d met once at a picnic. She wrote about nothing. That was the thing. The weather on Genesee Avenue. Her sister’s wedding.
tom-m7: I landed in California in my uniform, and by the time I got to Detroit I was in jeans and a sweatshirt. I changed in a restroom. Nobody told me to. I’d seen how people looked at the guys in uniform, and I’d had enough of being looked at for one year. My mother cried at the gate. My father shook my hand and held on a long time.
tom-m8: We got married at St. Joseph’s in June of ’71, the same parish as the picnic. Four years from lemonade to the altar, and I was gone for one of them and quiet for two. She waited through all three. People ask what I saw in her and I tell them the truth. I married the handwriting.
tom-m9: I refused for thirty years. Mike would bring it up and I’d change the subject. Then one morning at breakfast Diane told me I was going to Washington on the Honor Flight out of mid-Michigan in October, and Mike was going as my guardian, and it was done. I found out later who filled out the form. Hannah says she just filled it out.
tom-m10: The GI Bill paid for school, and the only thing I knew how to do was what I’d done over there. So I went to nursing school. There were two men in my class of thirty-eight. The other one quit by Christmas. I worked emergency for thirty-six years, mostly nights, because nights were quiet until they weren’t, and I was good when they weren’t.
tom-m11: Hannah asked me in 2020, for a history project, and I told her no. I told her it wasn’t a story for a kid. She said, then when? I didn’t have an answer. In 2025 she asked again. My friends from that year are mostly gone.
tom-m12: The first Memorial Day after the Wall, I went to the VFW for the reading of the names. They read the county boys, and then the commander asks if anybody has a name from somewhere else. I’d driven past that post for forty years. I’d never been in. I stood up and said, Daniel Alvarez, Corpus Christi, Texas, May 6, 1968. My voice held. Diane’s hand didn’t.
